item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
item.description:
Humans have trouble with inhuman distances. Miles are about the largest comprehensible unit of measurement we have, because we can understand miles. Watering hole is in a mile? No problem, we’ll be there soon. Aurochs herd is 30 miles away? OK, our hunting party won't walk that in a day, but it’s doable. Miles are a good measure for us, and on the scale of the universe, absolutely useless. The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Can that possibly be spatially encompassed by a human mind that evolved to think in terms of footsteps? The nearest star after that is about 25 trillion miles away. We have the words, but they blur into a meaningless litany of zeroes and -illions. How big is the observable universe? 546,710,000,000,000,000,000,000 miles across, best we can tell. What does that mean to us? Nothing. I submit that while it’s less accurate, it’s more truthful to say simply…

item.title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
item.description:
At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths. The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army , the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant. Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action. The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R.
